title: Gutenberg's Bible
hook: a goldsmith's press in Mainz prints the Bible, and books start to get cheap

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople fell, and the last liturgy under the great dome turned out not to be the last. Your line was the last liturgy.

A tiny metal letter, the size of a fingernail, stands on its end. A capital I. Next to it, an n. Then another, and another, until a whole line sits in a wooden frame, backward, like a word seen in a mirror. Ink goes over it, paper comes down, a screw turns, and the page comes up with the words the right way round. Then the letters come apart and get set again for the next page. In a workshop in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg is doing this with the whole Bible.

Before the press, every Bible in Europe was copied by hand, the way Thomas à Kempis copied at his desk. Every copy was its own work, and precious. Gutenberg's idea was to make the letters movable: cast them in metal, line them up, print a page, then break them apart and use them again. His Bible was in Latin, the Bible the Western church read in worship. Its Genesis begins with the words the King James Bible gives as: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The pages were made to look like the best handwritten books: two columns, dark, even letters. Copies were often finished by hand, with red headings and painted capitals, so no two look quite the same. Then other presses followed, in other cities. Books got cheaper, and more people could own one. Later, reformers would print the Bible in German and English, in the languages people spoke at home, and tracts and sermons traveled fast. Christians argued, sometimes fiercely, over what all those readers should do with what they read. But the change underneath was simple. A Psalm says, "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." For a long time, that lamp sat in a church or a library. The press began to put it on kitchen tables.
screen: `COPIED BY HAND, ONE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of a book that changed something for you: maybe a Bible, a novel, or a book of poems someone handed you at the right time. Then think of one person who might need a book right now, a friend, a child, a coworker, someone on your street, and choose a book for them. If you pray, pray for them as you choose; if you don't, just hold them in mind.
Gutenberg's Bible. The Latin Bible printed with movable metal type in Mainz, part of a change that made books, and Bibles, cheaper to own.
Your line: words for everyone. Once one press worked, others followed, in other cities. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians often give Bibles as gifts at baptisms, confirmations, weddings and graduations, and Bible societies print and give away Bibles in many languages.

notes: Claims rule: no date, copy count or page count is stated (the outline hook's 'around 1455' is not spoken). The trapdoor's first floor corrects 'the first book ever printed' only implicitly; the script makes no 'first' claim. Confirm.
Gutenberg as a goldsmith in Mainz, Latin Vulgate text, two-column layout, hand rubrication and illumination after printing: standard accounts; confirm.
'Within a couple of generations' for vernacular printed Bibles (Luther's German, Tyndale's English) is a soft time phrase; cut if it breaks the claims rule.
'Before the press, a Bible was copied by hand' refers to Europe; block printing existed elsewhere. Confirm the framing is fair.
The hook spells 'In' from Genesis 1:1 (In principio in the Vulgate); the letters I and n are the opening of both Latin and English. Confirm.
original is null: no original-language word worth teaching for this day.
